name: Lena Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena, 58, and I'm a junior helping the qualified electrician with wiring and repairs in homes and businesses. I took a vocational certificate during a break from college stores work while caring for my father; I'm still below the experienced crew for speed and skill, with my tasks assigned and checked. This firm pays above the usual rate, my partner maintains sports grounds, and we have fourteen months of expenses saved, grown children living elsewhere and a rented house. There are plenty of electrical firms nearby, but I've never used AI; I'd like retirement to become a real choice, without a confirmed income amount or date that makes it affordable yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the office keep a little help if it really helps. I've never used AI, and I'd rather someone mark the drawing beside the bit I don't understand. A useful day for me is learning one thing properly, not having an opinion on every machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wages and our household money feel secure in that picture. The firm pays above the usual rate, we've got fourteen months of expenses saved and there are plenty of electrical employers nearby. I'm still a beginner, but I don't need to pretend I'm one missed shift from disaster to ask for patient teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid supervised wiring tasks actually offered. Starting this week I'd ask the qualified electrician to mark one unclear instruction on paper and check I could explain it before I began. Through the first year my partner and I would keep our ordinary budget, counting no pension payment or grown child's wage we hadn't confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our living, and relieved that learning can stay a human conversation. I still get frustrated when I'm slow with a fitting. That's different from being frightened of the bill waiting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What brought you into the trade at 58?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had a break from college stores work to care for my father, and took a vocational certificate before returning to a job. I'm now a junior, below the experienced workers for speed and skill, with my tasks assigned and checked by someone qualified. Better pay at this firm doesn't give me a licence or permission to sign a job off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does home look like now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner maintains sports grounds, our two children are grown and living elsewhere, and we rent a small house. We built the reserve over years before this change in work. I'd like retirement to become an affordable choice, but I don't have confirmed income amounts and start dates that make it one today.

say: I'd accept **small office help** while choosing a paper explanation for my own unfamiliar tasks.
I'd value **one thing learned** properly more than an opinion on every new machine.
think: Our **higher wage and reserve** make the household secure, with fourteen months saved and plenty of nearby electrical employers.
I'm still a **junior learner**, but patient teaching needn't depend on pretending our next bill is a disaster.
do: Keep **offered paid supervised tasks** through the first year.
Ask for **marked paper instructions** and a qualified check of my understanding before unfamiliar work.
Keep the **ordinary budget**, counting no unconfirmed pension or grown child's earnings as ours.
feel: **Calm** about household money, with ordinary frustration at learning slowly separate from fear of the next bill.
S0.quote: Better pay at this firm doesn't give me a licence or permission to sign a job off.
fieldNote: Her **higher pay** and fourteen-month reserve support security without changing junior standing, below-average practical skill or her vocational certificate only.
She prefers **paper teaching**, has never used AI and keeps retirement affordability separate from age, family care history or grown children's earnings.

steps.text: Keep offered paid supervised tasks with marked paper instructions and qualified checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster schedules should still include time to teach the person holding the cable. I'd join other beginners asking for that time and the paid hours to be clear. I don't want the worker who asks twice treated as the waste a computer has found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own paid shifts and my partner's physical grounds work to hold over the next few years here. I'm uneasy about learners being rushed and the office staff losing a say in their own day. My reserve gives me room to ask a question, not evidence that a worker with less money should stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign a request with other beginners at this month's branch lunch meeting, without missing paid work, asking for paid practical teaching and written weekly hours and wages. I'd keep my paper method and ask a person to explain any required new procedure inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. In the first year I'd keep supervised work and compare the employer's actual written answer with what happened, assuming no agreement from a friendly reply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how people are treated, but secure about our own bills. I don't need to like a new screen to recognise that somebody needs a fair chance to learn it. I'd rather make the request before a frightened worker had to ask alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI if the branch preferred it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as part of this plan. I've never used AI, and I'd ask for the task and requirements explained personally before deciding about any genuinely new duty. Signing a request for paid teaching isn't agreeing to every tool someone might name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the written employer answer need to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which practical teaching happened in paid time, the weekly paid hours and wages, and who checked the beginner's work. I'd read the actual terms rather than a promise that nobody would be left behind. A kind sentence isn't a paid teaching hour.

I'd join a **beginners' request** for written paid hours and wages, without asking everyone to like the same tools.
think: Our **physical wages** look secure near term, supported by the reserve and local options.
I'm uneasy about **rushed learners** and office decisions, while having enough room to speak without an immediate household crisis.
do: Sign the **branch request** at lunch without missing paid work, seeking paid practical teaching and written weekly hours and wages.
Request **personal instruction** for required new procedures inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained, choosing no AI tool.
Keep **supervised work** and compare actual written terms with events, assuming no agreement from a polite reply.
feel: **Uneasy** about treatment of learners, with present household security and a specific shared request to make.
S1.quote: A kind sentence isn't a paid teaching hour.
fieldNote: Her **collective action** is an actual signed beginners' request, not merely individual instruction or an assumed employer concession.
Her **AI resistance** remains intact, while required work instruction has paid-time, normal-weekly-wage and qualified-checking conditions rather than unpaid goodwill.

steps.text: Sign lunch-meeting request without missing paid work for paid teaching and written weekly hours and wages
Keep supervised work and require personal instruction inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch thinking AI arrives in 2028, when I'll be 60, and capable robots around 2031, when I'll be 63. I'd want paid work discussed before a purchase decides who remains on the van. I'd tell the family we have time to check, not that our savings make us exceptions to the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior hours could shrink once robots can do the simple physical tasks I'm still learning. My partner's grounds work could face the same change, and I don't know the machine prices or each employer's pace. Fourteen months saved is room to choose, not lifetime income or a confirmed pension at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put 150 monthly from genuinely spare new wages into the reserve now, only after essentials and with my partner's agreement, leaving the existing fourteen-month reserve untouched. I'd request branch budget help to check actual retirement eligibility, amounts and dates, asking about availability rather than assuming an appointment. In 2029 I'd keep only offered paid supervised work within my actual ability, and stop the extra deposit if the spare money or agreement disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our later earnings, but not cornered into the first answer. I'd rather use the reserve to ask carefully than buy a course to prove I'd reacted. I can need a clear drawing and still read a household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the 150 money you already had saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would be a new monthly deposit from wages after ordinary costs, not moving the old reserve between accounts. If the budget didn't leave 150 or my partner stopped agreeing, the extra transfer would stop. I won't borrow to make a savings target look obedient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would checking retirement figures mean choosing to leave work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what I actually qualified for, when income could start and what the amount covered. We'd use confirmed figures before any decision. Retirement isn't a payment just because the calendar has brought it nearer.

I'd tell the **family** we have room to check, without claiming the reserve makes our jobs exempt.
think: Both **physical household jobs** could lose hours when robots reach simple tasks.
Our **fourteen-month reserve** gives choice time, not lifetime wages or a confirmed pension at a birthday.

Request **branch budget help**, checking availability and actual retirement eligibility, amounts and dates without assuming an appointment.
Keep **offered paid supervised work** within actual ability in 2029, stopping the extra deposit if surplus or partner consent ends.

S2.quote: I won't borrow to make a savings target look obedient.
fieldNote: Her **new deposits** use future wage surplus, preserve existing savings and stop if surplus or partner consent disappears.
Her **retirement enquiry** creates neither eligibility nor an exit, while first-year work stays conditional on actual paid offers, supervision and ability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the branch time to ask what practical learning and paid roles actually exist. Thinking AI arrives at 63 in 2031, then robots at about 66 in 2034. I'd want older beginners in the discussion, not treated as though every question could be answered by telling us to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current physical wages look steady over the next few years, and we have a substantial reserve and plenty of employers nearby. The later question is still on my mind because I don't know what income would make stopping affordable. More warning gives time to get facts, not a rule that my body or a pension lasts for whatever the budget needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the signed branch request and the 150 monthly saving now only under the same surplus, partner-consent and untouched-reserve conditions. I'd request available budget help to obtain actual income eligibility, amounts and start dates. In 2032 my partner and I would review confirmed resources and my actual ability before choosing among real paid supervised options or an affordable exit, with no exit decision unless the budget worked and my partner agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later life, but secure enough now to take a question slowly. I'd like to stop working at some point without pretending the decision is already paid for. I'd also like the person with a smaller reserve to get the same clear answer from the employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be an electrical worker at 64 in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't promise a job or what my health would allow. We'd check the actual offers and the tasks I could do under required supervision. I wouldn't write a wage into the gap just because I had learned to carry the toolbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the branch to include for people without your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time, an instructor who can check the task and written weekly wages and hours. I'd sign that request with the other beginners, without missing paid work. A beginner's need for patient teaching doesn't get smaller because their bank balance does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to plan with real information rather than sell every older worker the same stopping date. Thinking AI would come at 68 in 2036 and robots around 71 in 2039. I'd still want paid learning available now, including to the person who can't buy time from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages and fourteen-month reserve make the next few years feel secure. I don't know whether I'd be able to stop before 2036 or still need income then, and I won't assume the children fund a shortfall. The later question stays with me without making today's rent an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep requesting the branch's written paid-learning terms now and save 150 monthly only while essentials, partner consent and the untouched reserve conditions held. I'd keep paid supervised tasks only where offered and within my actual ability now. In 2037 we'd use actual resources, living costs and capacity before deciding among real paid options or an affordable exit, with my partner's agreement rather than an assumed job at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what later life requires, but able to enjoy the time we have now. I don't need to pretend I like AI to help ask for a usable route. I can have savings without pretending the rest of the workforce can live on patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you assume about your grown children then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only what they actually offered and could manage, not a wage or a room I'd put in the budget without asking. They have their own families and costs. My grown children don't owe me a retirement wage because I'm their parent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your partner no longer agreed with the extra saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra deposit would stop, just as it would if essentials used the surplus. We'd keep the old reserve separate and talk about what had changed. Agreement is something to keep checking, not a permission slip for the next decade.

I can't assume **adult-child income**, a job at 69 or pension money closes the future household budget.

Check **2037 resources and capacity** before real paid options or any exit, requiring confirmed affordability and partner agreement rather than assumed employment.
feel: **Uneasy** about later uncertainty, with current security and a shared plan that preserves both consent and a real financial buffer.
S4.quote: My grown children don't owe me a retirement wage because I'm their parent.
fieldNote: Her **long warning** leaves future pensions, jobs and child support unconfirmed while current pay and savings provide real comfort.
Her **extra deposits** still require real surplus and continuing consent; actual resources and capacity must support any later exit decision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could shrink our physical-work hours before we know what could replace the wages. Paid practical teaching, written weekly hours and wages, and real income figures would help. I'd want those answers available to an older beginner with no reserve too, not just somebody who can afford to ask slowly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether having savings makes a person obliged to stop asking about fair treatment. My reserve can buy time, but it can't teach the person the firm won't pay to train. I can need a simple drawing and still know what an unpaid promise costs another household.

headlineQuote: My reserve can buy time, but it can't teach the person the firm won't pay to train.
portrait: **Lena, 58**, is a junior with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and supervised tasks after a family-care career break.
She has **higher pay**, fourteen months saved, plenty of local employers, a grounds-worker partner and grown children whose earnings are not assumed.
She has **never used AI**, preferring paper explanations while joining beginners' requests for paid practical teaching and written weekly wages and hours.
Her **new wage deposits** require surplus after essentials, continuing partner consent and an untouched reserve; later work or an exit remains unconfirmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before robots around 2031 could reduce both physical incomes, while retirement affordability remains unknown.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid teaching** and written terms would clarify real weekly wages and hours.
Actual **income records** with eligibility, amounts and start dates would support decisions without assumed child payments.
